properties.description:
FFWFFC

The National Weather Service in Peachtree City has issued a

* Flash Flood Warning for...
Clayton County in north central Georgia...
DeKalb County in north central Georgia...
Central Fulton County in north central Georgia...
Southwestern Gwinnett County in north central Georgia...
Northwestern Henry County in north central Georgia...
Central Rockdale County in north central Georgia...

* Until 115 PM EDT Saturday.

* At 712 AM EDT, Doppler radar indicated thunderstorms producing
heavy rain across the warned area. Between 1 and 3 inches of rain
have fallen. Additional rainfall amounts of 2 to 3 inches are
possible in the warned area. Flash flooding is ongoing or expected
to begin shortly.

HAZARD...Flash flooding caused by heavy rain.

SOURCE...Radar indicated.

IMPACT...Flash flooding of small creeks and streams, urban areas,
highways, streets and underpasses as well as other poor
drainage and low-lying areas.

* Some locations that will experience flash flooding include...
Atlanta, McDonough, Decatur, Jonesboro, Peachtree Corners, Sandy
Springs, Johns Creek, Dunwoody, East Point, Duluth, Stockbridge,
Forest Park, Riverdale, College Park, Lilburn, Chamblee, Norcross
and Doraville.

deaths occur in vehicles.

properties.headline: Tropical Cyclone Local Statement issued October 10 at 2:40AM PDT by NWS San Diego CA
properties.description:
HLSSGX

This product covers EXTREME SOUTHWESTERN CALIFORNIA

**Tropical Storm Rachel Will Bring Coastal Flooding, Wind, and Rain
to Portions of Southern California Sunday**

NEW INFORMATION
---------------

* CHANGES TO WATCHES AND WARNINGS:
- None

* CURRENT WATCHES AND WARNINGS:
- A Tropical Storm Watch is in effect for San Diego County
Coastal Areas, San Diego County Deserts, San Diego County
Mountains, and San Diego County Valleys

* STORM INFORMATION:
- About 670 miles south-southwest of San Mateo Point CA or about
630 miles south-southwest of Mouth of Tijuana River CA
- 24.2N 121.4W
- Storm Intensity 60 mph
- Movement Northeast or 50 degrees at 22 mph

SITUATION OVERVIEW
------------------

Tropical Storm Rachel is currently about 600 miles southwest of San
Diego, moving northeast towards Northern Baja at about 19 kts. Rachel
is expected to make landfall somewhere just south of the US/Mexico
Border Saturday evening. Tropical storm level impacts will likely
affect San Diego County. A Tropical Storm Watch is in effect for all of
San Diego County. The main concerns with Tropical Storm Rachel are
coastal flooding, wind, and periods of heavy rain which could lead to
localized flooding and flash flooding. The majority of impacts from the
tropical storm are expected on Sunday.

South swell from Tropical Storm Rachel will arrive on Sunday. The
combination of south and northwest swells, increased onshore winds,
and high tides over 7 feet will maintain a threat of coastal flooding
and beach erosion along beaches in San Diego and Orange Counties. Surf
on Sunday is currently expected to peak at 6 to 9 feet, decreasing to
3 to 6 feet for Monday and Tuesday. Confidence in impactful coastal
flooding is high, with significant coastal flooding and beach erosion
likely.

Widespread rain is expected on Sunday from Tropical Storm Rachel.
There is expected to be a gradient in rainfall amounts with the higher
amounts on the southeastern side of the storm. Confidence is high that
the heaviest rain will occur over San Diego County mountains and
deserts. Peak rainfall rates of 0.50 to 0.60 inches are possible for
the coast and valleys, 0.50 to 0.70 inches per hour possible for the
deserts, and 0.70 to 1 inch per hour for the mountains. Current
forecast has rainfall totals of 0.50 to 1.25 inches for the coast,
valleys, and deserts and 1 to 2.5 inches for the mountains. Areas of
flash and urban flooding are probable, especially where the maximum
rainfall rates occur. The San Diego River at Fashion Valley is
currently forecast to peak at 7.4 feet (just below monitor stage)
Sunday afternoon. Those with interests near the San Diego River should
continue to monitor the forecast.

Increased winds are expected with the onset and passage of Tropical
Storm Rachel. Sustained winds of 39+ mph are expected on the southeast
side of the storm. Based on the current track, more southern and
eastern parts of San Diego County are most likely to see winds of this
magnitude. Regardless, strong sustained winds and wind gusts can be
expected on Sunday. Winds will likely be enhanced by local terrain
with gusts 40 to 55 mph on the desert slopes of the mountains and into
the deserts. Local gusts up to 60 mph possible on mountain ridges and
in passes and canyons.

POTENTIAL IMPACTS
-----------------

* WIND:
Prepare for hazardous wind having possible limited impacts across
EXTREME SOUTHWESTERN CALIFORNIA. Potential impacts in this area
include:
- Damage to porches, awnings, carports, sheds, and unanchored
mobile homes. Unsecured lightweight objects blown about.
- Many large tree limbs broken off. A few trees snapped or
uprooted, but with greater numbers in places where trees are
shallow rooted, especially in coastal and valley locations that
don't typically experience strong winds. Some fences and
roadway signs blown over.
- A few roads impassable from debris, particularly within urban
or heavily wooded places. Hazardous driving conditions on
bridges and other elevated roadways.
- Scattered power and communications outages.

Elsewhere across EXTREME SOUTHWESTERN CALIFORNIA, little to no impact
is anticipated.

* FLOODING RAIN:
Prepare for life-threatening rainfall flooding having possible
extensive impacts across San Diego County. Potential impacts include:
- Major rainfall flooding may prompt many evacuations and rescues.
- Rivers and tributaries may rapidly overflow their banks in
multiple places. Small streams, creeks, canals, arroyos, and
ditches may become dangerous rivers. In mountain areas,
destructive runoff may run quickly down valleys while
increasing susceptibility to rockslides and mudslides. Flood
control systems and barriers may become stressed.
- Flood waters can enter many structures within multiple
communities, some structures becoming uninhabitable or washed
away. Many places where flood waters may cover escape routes.
Streets and parking lots become rivers of moving water with
underpasses submerged. Driving conditions become dangerous.

----------------------------------

* OTHER PREPAREDNESS INFORMATION:

kit and take necessary actions to protect your family and secure your
home or business.

When making safety and preparedness decisions, do not focus on the
exact forecast track since hazards such as flooding rain, damaging
wind gusts, storm surge, and tornadoes extend well away from the
center of the storm.

If in a place that is vulnerable to high wind, such as near large
trees, a manufactured home, upper floors of a high-rise building, or
on a boat, plan to move to safe shelter.

If you live in a place particularly vulnerable to flooding, such as
near the ocean or a large inland lake, in a low-lying or poor
drainage area, in a valley, or near an already swollen river, plan to
move to safe shelter on higher ground.

Always heed the advice of local officials and comply with orders that
are issued. Do not needlessly jeopardize your life or the lives of
others.

When securing your property, outside preparations should be concluded
as soon as possible before conditions deteriorate. The onset of
strong gusty winds or flooding can cause certain preparedness
activities to become unsafe.

Be sure to let friends and family members know of your intentions for
weathering the storm and your whereabouts. Have someone located away
from the threatened area serve as your point of contact. Share vital
contact information with others. Keep cell phones handy and charged.

Check on those who may not be fully aware of the situation or who are
unable to make personal preparations.

If you are a visitor, know the name of the county or parish in which
you are located and where it is relative to current watches and
warnings. If staying at a hotel, ask the management staff about their
onsite disaster plan. Listen for evacuation orders, especially
pertaining to area visitors.

Closely monitor weather.gov, NOAA Weather Radio and local news
outlets for official storm information. Listen for possible changes
to the forecast.

There is a threat from tornadoes with this storm. Have multiple ways
to receive Tornado Warnings. Be ready to shelter quickly.

This product covers North and Central Georgia

**ISAIAS MOVING INLAND OVER ALABAMA**
**FLASH FLOODING AND TORNADO RISKS CONTINUE INTO TONIGHT**

NEW INFORMATION
---------------

* CHANGES TO WATCHES AND WARNINGS:
- The Tropical Storm Warning has been cancelled for
Chattahoochee, Harris, Heard, Macon, Marion, Meriwether,
Muscogee, Pike, Schley, Stewart, Sumter, Talbot, Taylor, Troup,
Upson, and Webster

- About 170 miles southwest of Atlanta GA or about 90 miles
west-southwest of Columbus GA
- 32.0N 86.5W
- Storm Intensity 35 mph
- Movement North or 360 degrees at 14 mph

SITUATION OVERVIEW
------------------

As of 5 AM EDT, Post-Tropical Cyclone Isaias was moving northward
across Alabama at 14 MPH with maximum sustained winds of 35 MPH.
Widespread and potentially significant impacts are starting to unfold
across North and Central Georgia on the eastern side of Isaias. These
include a prolonged period of strong winds, heavy rainfall with
localized flooding, and the potential for several tornadoes. Impacts
will peak in intensity today into tonight as Isaias continues moving
north across Alabama and into the Tennessee Valley.

While Isaias is weakening and has become post-tropical, there will be
a very strong pressure gradient between the system and strong high
pressure over the Mid-Atlantic. This gradient will support a prolonged
period of strong easterly winds with frequent gusts to 40 to 50 mph
across most of North Georgia through this afternoon and into tonight.
A High Wind Warning is in effect for this area. Areas to the south of
these warnings are in a Wind Advisory where winds will be weaker,
though gusts up to 40 mph will be possible. Across all areas, the
prolonged and strong winds could lead to power outages from downed
limbs and trees, especially when combined with saturated soils from
periods of heavy rain.

Isaias will continue to bring widespread rainfall to the area, with
multiple bands of heavy rain expected through early Sunday. Widespread
rainfall totals of 2 to 4 inches are likely across much of the area. A
localized swath of as much as 8 inches will be possible where the
heaviest banding sets up. This rainfall could lead to flash flooding,
particularly in urban and poor-drainge areas, as well as flood-prone
creeks and streams. The north-south orientation of bands may enhance
river flooding along north-south reaches. Training heavy rain in the
mountains may furthermore increase the risk of landslides. A Flood
Watch remains in effect for the entire area, as a result.

Additionally, a favorable environment for tornadoes is starting to
develop across Central Georgia early this morning, and will advance
into north Georgia by the afternoon and evening. Several tornadoes will
be possible, particularly within the outer rainbands of the system.
Tornadoes from tropical systems are typically quick to develop and
short-lived, but with the forward speed of the system and the unique
setup, we can't rule out a stronger (EF2 or EF3), long-track tornado,
especially across Central Georgia.

POTENTIAL IMPACTS
-----------------

* WIND:
Potential impacts from the main wind event are now unfolding across
North and Central Georgia. Remain well sheltered from hazardous wind
having potentially significant impacts. If realized, these impacts
include:
- Damage to porches, awnings, carports, sheds, and unanchored
mobile homes. Unsecured lightweight objects blown about.
- Many large tree limbs broken off. A few trees snapped or
uprooted, but with greater numbers in places where trees are
shallow rooted. Some fences and roadway signs blown over.
- A few roads impassable from debris, particularly within urban
or heavily wooded places. Hazardous driving conditions on
bridges and other elevated roadways.
- Scattered power and communications outages.

* FLOODING RAIN:
Potential impacts from the flooding rain are still unfolding across
North and Central Georgia. Remain well guarded against life-
threatening flood waters having possible extensive impacts. If
realized, these impacts include:
- Major rainfall flooding may prompt many evacuations and rescues.
- Rivers and tributaries may rapidly overflow their banks in
multiple places. Small streams, creeks, canals, arroyos, and
ditches may become dangerous rivers. In mountain areas,
destructive runoff may run quickly down valleys while
increasing susceptibility to rockslides and mudslides. Flood
control systems and barriers may become stressed.
- Flood waters can enter many structures within multiple
communities, some structures becoming uninhabitable or washed
away. Many places where flood waters may cover escape routes.
Streets and parking lots become rivers of moving water with
underpasses submerged. Driving conditions become dangerous. Many
road and bridge closures with some weakened or washed out.

* TORNADOES:
Potential impacts from tornadoes are still unfolding across North and
Central Georgia. Remain well braced against a dangerous tornado event
having possible significant impacts. If realized, these impacts
include:
- The occurrence of scattered tornadoes can hinder the execution
of emergency plans during tropical events.
- Several places may experience tornado damage with a few spots
of considerable damage, power loss, and communications failures.
- Locations could realize roofs torn off frame houses, mobile
homes demolished, boxcars overturned, large trees snapped or
uprooted, vehicles tumbled, and small boats tossed about.
Dangerous projectiles can add to the toll.

PRECAUTIONARY/PREPAREDNESS ACTIONS
----------------------------------

* EVACUATIONS:
Follow the advice of local officials.

* OTHER PREPAREDNESS INFORMATION:
Now is the time to stay inside and away from windows. Listen for
updates and be ready in case you lose electrical power. Keep a battery-
powered radio, charged cell phone and flashlight handy.

During the peak of the storm be ready to move quickly. Keep your
shoes on and rain gear handy. Boots and athletic shoes offer the best
foot protection if you become unexpectedly exposed to the weather.

Keep your cell phone charged and in power-saving mode. If you lose
power, use it sparingly and mainly for personal emergencies and
check-ins.

If you are prone to flooding or in an area under a storm surge watch
or warning, be prepared for the possibility of a quick and dramatic
rise in water levels.

If a tornado warning is issued for your area, quickly move to the
safest place within your shelter. Protect your head and body.

The previous Storm Surge Warning has been replaced by a Coastal Flood

inundation values of 1 to 3 feet above normally dry ground are possible

Very heavy rain was observed earlier this evening mainly along and
just east of Isaias' track. Radar-estimated amounts highlight a swath

and Coffee County, AL with isolated amounts in excess of 10 inches.

flooding rain threat has subsided, additional bands of showers with
embedded heavy rain are expected to focus across the Forgotten Coast,
Florida Big Bend, and I-75 corridor. A Flood Watch remains in effect
for points east of US-19.

The tornado risk has also diminished substantially overnight, but
there is another window of opportunity for potential tornadic
circulations within the aforementioned bands through this afternoon.

Despite the overall improved weather conditions, residents are urged
to remain vigilant with respect to damage in the form of downed trees
and power lines, in addition to any standing water from flooding rains,
and continued hazardous beach conditions.Listen to local officials
during any cleanup efforts. Exercise caution if affected by power
outages.

-----------------

Check on your neighbors. If necessary, help them connect with their

continued flooding in low lying areas and non-functioning traffic

Do not go sightseeing within impacted communities. Sightseers
interfere with the emergency work of first responders.

leaking flammables.

be especially dangerous. If you are not in good health or unsure
about what you are doing, have someone with tree cutting experience
do the job. Never cut trees without a partner.

instructions provided by the manufacturer. Operate your generator in
a well-ventilated space outside of your living area and away from
open doors and windows.

Concern Today**

---------------

------------------

in effect for those affected areas.

Mississippi, Northeast Louisiana, and extreme Southeast Arkansas.

Mississippi, Northeast Louisiana, and extreme Southeast Arkansas.

Mississippi, Northeast Louisiana, and extreme Southeast Arkansas.

wiring, broken glass, jagged metal and wood, and protruding nails and
screws.

Be alert for any lingering wind gusts which could take down weakened
trees and/or power lines, collapse damaged structures, or cause
flying debris.

HLSMEG

**THE REMNANTS OF ISAIAS WILL CONTINUE TO MOVE NORTH OVERNIGHT**

NEW INFORMATION
---------------

* CHANGES TO WATCHES AND WARNINGS:
- All watches and warnings have been canceled

* CURRENT WATCHES AND WARNINGS:
- None

* STORM INFORMATION:
- About 320 miles southeast of Memphis TN or about 230 miles
southeast of Tupelo MS
- 31.5N 86.5W
- Storm Intensity 65 mph
- Movement North or 355 degrees at 20 mph

SITUATION OVERVIEW
------------------

Hurricane Isaias made landfall around 8:30 PM CDT this evening near
Destin, FL and quickly became post-tropical. Its remnants will move
inland through Saturday, bringing gusty winds and heavy rainfall across
portions of the Mid-South. A wind advisory will replace the Tropical
Storm Warning and a flooding threat continues.

POTENTIAL IMPACTS
-----------------

* WIND:
Protect against hazardous wind having possible limited impacts across
northeast Mississippi. Potential impacts in this area include:
- Damage to porches, awnings, carports, sheds, and unanchored
mobile homes. Unsecured lightweight objects blown about.
- Many large tree limbs broken off. A few trees snapped or
uprooted, but with greater numbers in places where trees are
shallow rooted. Some fences and roadway signs blown over.
- A few roads impassable from debris, particularly within urban
or heavily wooded places. Hazardous driving conditions on
bridges and other elevated roadways.
- Scattered power and communications outages.

Elsewhere across Mid-South, little to no impact is anticipated.

* FLOODING RAIN:
Protect against dangerous rainfall flooding having possible significant
impacts across northeast Mississippi. Potential impacts include:
- Moderate rainfall flooding may prompt several evacuations and
rescues.
- Rivers and tributaries may quickly become swollen with swifter
currents and overspill their banks in a few places, especially
in usually vulnerable spots. Small streams, creeks, canals,
arroyos, and ditches overflow.
- Flood waters can enter some structures or weaken foundations.
Several places may experience expanded areas of rapid
inundation at underpasses, low-lying spots, and poor drainage
areas. Some streets and parking lots take on moving water as
storm drains and retention ponds overflow. Driving conditions
become hazardous. Some road and bridge closures.

Protect against locally hazardous rainfall flooding having possible
limited impacts across northeast Mississippi.

- For information on creating an emergency plan see getagameplan.org
- For additional disaster preparedness information see redcross.org

NEXT UPDATE
-----------

Service in Memphis TN as conditions warrant.

------------------

At 2 AM ET, Post-Tropical Cyclone Isaias was moving north at 20 mph
over Southern Alabama with max sustained winds of 65 mph. All prior
Hurricane Warnings have been replaced by Tropical Storm Warnings to
account for lingering gusty winds occasionally to around 40 mph or
higher. Other pre-existing hazards remain in effect through this
intermediate advisory cycle.

A Storm Surge Warning continues across all of our Florida Panhandle
and Big Bend coast until later this morning for inundation values of
2 to 4 feet above normally dry ground. Coastal saltwater flooding may
linger through Saturday from persistent onshore flow.

Very heavy rain was observed earlier this evening mainly along and
just east of Isaias' track. Radar-estimated amounts highlight a swath
of 7 to 8 inches from coastal Walton County, FL into western Geneva,
and Coffee County, AL with isolated amounts in excess of 10 inches.
Standing water is likely at those locations. Although much of the
flooding rain threat has subsided, additional bands of showers with
embedded heavy rain are expected to redevelop later this morning and
focus across the Forgotten Coast, Florida Big Bend, and I-75 corridor.
A Flood Watch remains in effect areawide until this evening.

The tornado risk has also diminished substantially this evening, but
there is another window of opportunity for potential tornadic
circulations within the aforementioned bands through this afternoon.

Despite the overall improved weather conditions, residents are urged
to remain vigilant with respect to damage in the form of downed trees
and power lines, in addition to any standing water from flooding
rains, and continued hazardous beach conditions.

POTENTIAL IMPACTS
-----------------

* FLOODING RAIN:
Potential impacts from the flooding rain are still ongoing across
parts of the Tri-state area. Remain well guarded against life-
threatening flood waters having possible devastating impacts. If
realized, these impacts include:
- Extreme rainfall flooding may prompt numerous evacuations and
rescues.
- Rivers and tributaries may overwhelmingly overflow their banks
in many places with deep moving water. Small streams, creeks, and
ditches may become raging rivers. Flood control systems and
barriers may become stressed.
- Flood waters can enter numerous structures within multiple
communities, some structures becoming uninhabitable or washed
away. Numerous places where flood waters may cover escape routes.
Streets and parking lots become rivers of raging water with
underpasses submerged. Driving conditions become very dangerous.
Numerous road and bridge closures with some weakened or washed
out.

* SURGE:
Potential impacts from the main surge event are still ongoing across
the Florida Panhandle and Big Bend coast. Remain well away from life-
threatening surge having possible significant impacts. If realized,
these impacts include:
- Areas of inundation with storm surge flooding accentuated by
waves. Damage to several buildings, mainly near the coast.
- Sections of near-shore escape routes and secondary roads become
weakened or washed out, especially in usually vulnerable low
spots.
- Major beach erosion with heavy surf breaching dunes. Strong and
numerous rip currents.
- Moderate damage to marinas, docks, boardwalks, and piers.
Several small craft broken away from moorings, especially in
unprotected anchorages.

* TORNADOES:
Potential impacts from tornadoes possibly unfold across the Florida
Big Bend and parts of southwest Georgia. Remain well braced against a
dangerous tornado event having possible significant impacts. If
realized, these impacts include:
- The occurrence of scattered tornadoes can hinder the execution
of emergency plans during tropical events.
- Several places may experience tornado damage with a few spots of
considerable damage, power loss, and communications failures.
- Locations could realize roofs torn off frame houses, mobile
homes demolished, boxcars overturned, large trees snapped or
uprooted, vehicles tumbled, and small boats tossed about.
Dangerous projectiles can add to the toll.

* WIND:
Potential impacts from the main wind event are ongoing across much of
the Tri-state area. Remain well sheltered from strong to gusty winds
having possible devastating impacts. If realized, these impacts
include:
- Structural damage to sturdy buildings, some with complete roof
and wall failures. Complete destruction of mobile homes. Damage
greatly accentuated by large airborne projectiles. Locations may
be uninhabitable for weeks or months.
- Numerous large trees snapped or uprooted along with fences and
roadway signs blown over.
- Many roads impassable from large debris, and more within urban
or heavily wooded places. Many bridges, causeways, and access
routes impassable.
- Widespread power and communications outages.

PRECAUTIONARY/PREPAREDNESS ACTIONS
----------------------------------

* EVACUATIONS:
Follow the advice of local officials

* OTHER PREPAREDNESS INFORMATION:

Keep your cell phone charged and in power-saving mode. If you lose
power, use it sparingly and mainly for personal emergencies and
check-ins.

Do not be a thrill seeker or risk your life for senseless photos or
videos.

If you are prone to flooding or in an area under a storm surge watch
or warning, be prepared for the possibility of a quick and dramatic
rise in water levels.

Post-Tropical Cyclone Isaias with winds of 65 mph will continue to

wind impacts still exist east of the Alabama River, excluding Baldwin
county, with the strongest winds occurring across the northeast
portion of our warning area closest to the decaying center of
circulation. Potential impacts from these winds include downed trees
and power lines, and power outages. Storm surge will remain elevated
along the Okaloosa county coast through late tonight.

-----------------

* WIND:
Protect against strong wind gusts having possible additional impacts
east of the Alabama river, excluding Baldwin county. Potential impacts
in this area include:
- Minor structural damage.
- Some large trees snapped or uprooted along with fences and
roadway signs blown over.
- Some roads impassable due to debris, and more within urban
or heavily wooded places.
- Widespread power and communications outages.

coastal Okaloosa county. Potential impacts in this area include:
- Areas of inundation, mainly near the coast.

weakened or washed out, especially in usually vulnerable low
spots.

numerous rip currents.

can be helpful, but be aware of your risk for deadly carbon monoxide
poisoning if your car is left idling in a garage or other poorly
ventilated area.

It is important to remain calm, informed, and focused during an
emergency. Be patient and helpful with those you encounter.

Rising flood waters are deadly. If you are in a flood-prone
area, consider moving to higher ground. Never drive through a
flooded roadway. Remember, turn around don't drown!

If in a place that is vulnerable to high wind, such as near large
trees, a manufactured home, upper floors of a high-rise building, or
on a boat, consider moving to a safer shelter before the onset of
strong winds or flooding.

Closely monitor weather.gov, NOAA Weather radio or local news outlets
for official storm information. Be ready to adapt to possible changes
to the forecast. Ensure you have multiple ways to receive weather
warnings.

...The National Weather Service in Greenville-Spartanburg has issued

Haywood County.

.Heavy rainfall from the remnants of Hurricane Isaias will result in
excessive runoff and significant rises on streams within the upper
Pigeon River watershed.  Rainfall will develop overnight tonight,
intensify during the day on Saturday, and maintain intensity
overnight Saturday before tapering off by early Sunday morning.

inches possible, across the upper Pigeon River watershed, generally
upstream of Canton.  The highest totals will occur along the Pisgah
ridge and in the Shining Rock and Middle Prong Wilderness areas
within the headwaters of the east and west forks of the Pigeon River,

the timing and amounts of the heaviest rainfall, there is enough
confidence in the current forecast that out-of-bank conditions are
likely for the Pigeon River.  Therefore, a River Flood Advisory has
been issued for the reach near Canton, with a crest above Action
Stage expected Sunday morning.  A rise above Action Stage will result
in nuisance, relatively shallow flooding of low-lying areas adjacent
to the Pigeon River, including farmland, woodlands, low-lying
secondary roads, greenways, parks, and other flood-prone locations.

More significant rises along the Pigeon River are possible, and those
with interests along the river are encouraged to stay weather aware
and up-to-date on the latest stream levels and forecasts at
https://water.noaa.gov/wfo/GSP.  Current reasonable worst-case
scenarios are posted in the ADDITIONAL DETAILS sections below.
Forecast crests above Minor Flood Stage may result in the River Flood
Advisories being upgraded to River Flood Warnings.

* WHAT...Flooding caused by excessive rainfall is expected.

* WHERE...Pigeon River at above Old River Rd (NC 215), 1 SW Canton.

* WHEN...From this evening to late Sunday night.

* IMPACTS...At 8.0 feet, Action/Advisory Stage.  Common, nuisance
flooding of low-lying areas adjacent to the Pigeon River is
beginning.  Floodwaters are beginning to impact farmland,
woodlands, nurseries, parks, athletic fields, golf courses,
greenways, and boat-access areas with up to 2 feet of inundation.
Low-water crossings may be inundated with up to 2 feet of
floodwater and become impassable.  Adjacent campgrounds, mobile
home/RV parks, and secondary roads may experience floodwater
inundation of up to 1 foot.

* ADDITIONAL DETAILS...
- At 11:45 PM EDT Friday the stage was 1.2 feet and steady.

Sunday morning.  A reasonable worst-case crest above Minor Flood
Stage below 11 feet cannot be ruled out.

properties.description:
The following statement was issued by the Oklahoma Department of
Environmental Quality until 10 PM CDT Saturday evening.

An Air Quality Alert for Ozone has been issued for Friday, October
9th, and Saturday, October 10th, for the Oklahoma City Metropolitan
area due to expected high concentrations of ozone.

Public Health Recommendations: Persons with existing heart or
respiratory ailments should reduce physical exertion and outdoor
activity.

The general public is encouraged to help alleviate the problem by
reducing vehicle miles traveled by riding the bus, carpooling, or
avoiding unnecessary trips. The public is also asked to avoid
refueling during the morning and early afternoon hours, and to avoid
the use of two cycle engines such as lawn mowers, motorcycles, weed
trimmers, and outboard engines. It is also advised to limit outdoor
burning.

To view the latest air quality map, visit airnow.gov or the AirNow
app.

For hourly updates on concentrations and possible health warnings,
telephone the Oklahoma Department of Environmental Quality at
405-702-4100. For more information on health effects, call the
American Lung Association of Oklahoma at 405-748-4674

properties.headline: Hydrologic Outlook issued October 9 at 10:53AM MDT by NWS Grand Junction CO
properties.description:
ESFGJT

A strong low pressure system off the Pacific Coast will begin to draw
in tropical moisture associated with Topical Storm Rachel this
weekend. This strong southerly fetch will draw anomalously high
moisture content across the Desert Southwest and into eastern Utah
and western Colorado. The chance for widespread precipitation
increases Saturday evening into Sunday. Total precipitation forecasts
range from 1 to 3 inches across high terrain, with highest amounts
favoring the Uintas, Tavaputs and the Southwest San Juan mountains.

Embedded thunderstorms are also possible Sunday afternoon, increasing
the threat for flash flooding across vulnerable terrain. While
confidence in location and rainfall rates remain low at this time,
the potential for rapidly rising rivers, streams, normally dry
arroyos and slot canyons are possible Sunday through Monday.

Please follow the evolving forecast, especially if your plans
including recreating or commuting across eastern Utah and western
Colorado Sunday onward. Also, keep in mind weather potential above
your location and upstream, particularly for those who reside below
sensitive terrain like recent burn scars.
